title: The second arrow at home
hookLine: a ruined pen, an hour of stewing, and the two arrows (SN 36.6)
tomorrow: the Buddha gave five ways to drop a grudge. which one is the oddest?

cards: Someone at home borrowed your good pen and crushed the tip. It took one second to find out.
Then the hour after: replaying it, rehearsing what to say, deciding what it says about them, and about how nobody respects your things. By dinner it has grown into a whole case file, with exhibits.
The dishwasher loaded wrong last week is in there too. The pen is still just a pen. So why does it still sting an hour later?
The Buddha had a picture for that hour.

teach.b: In the Samyutta Nikaya, he describes someone struck by an arrow, and then struck right away by a second one. Two wounds instead of one. The first arrow is the painful thing itself: the ache, the loss, the crushed tip.
Everyone gets those, the Buddha says, the wise included.

teach.h: THE SECOND IS WHAT WE ADD.
teach.b: The second arrow is what the untrained mind adds: the sorrow, the complaining, the replay, the story. The one who's trained feels the first and doesn't fire the second. Home is a second-arrow factory.
Small things, close quarters, a history with everyone. Now a neighbor who says something close.

teach.h: THE GITA: THEY COME AND GO.
teach.b: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna that the touch of the senses brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain; they come and they go, they don't last, so bear them steadily.
Both see the same thing: the sensation arrives, and what you build on top of it is where the suffering grows. And an honest difference.
In the Gita, that steadiness serves Arjuna's duty, and rests on a self that, Krishna says, is never born and never dies.
The sutta trains the same steadiness without a lasting self underneath: a feeling, seen as just a feeling.
Two traditions, two foundations, one shared noticing.
The pen is the first arrow. The hour is the second, and that one is optional.

how: Some Buddhist teachers use the two arrows from SN 36.6 to teach mindfulness of feeling: noticing pain or annoyance as it is, without adding the mental reaction on top.

games.q: what does “the second arrow at home” mean?
o: a second annoyance that always follows a first
the extra hurt we add to a small sting by replaying it
a family member who hurts you twice in one day

games.q: two arrows, two traditions — tap the pairs.
p: the replay and the story we add
cold and heat come and go; bear them
an undying self, or none underneath

s: the trained person in the sutta feels no pain at all
the wise feel the first arrow too; they don't fire the second.
the Gita and the sutta both notice that sensations come and go
Krishna says bear them steadily; the Buddha says don't add the second arrow.
the Gita and the sutta rest on the same view of the self
the Gita speaks of a self never born and never dying; the sutta trains without one.

games.q: your sister ate the leftovers you were saving. it's gone, it's dinner time, and you're already drafting the speech. what's the second arrow here?
o: the empty container, which really is a loss.
the speech you're drafting and replaying in your head.
being hungry, which you shouldn't feel at all.
games.why: the missing food is the first arrow, and it's real. the speech on loop is the one you're adding, and that one you can set down.

practice: Pick one small annoyance from today. If you have paper, write the first arrow in a single plain line: what actually happened, nothing more.
Then notice the second arrow you've been adding, the replay and the story, and with one long breath out, set only that one down.

wordCard.voice: The second arrow at home: the extra pain we add to small annoyances, the replay after the sting.

orig.note: Pali: an arrow, a dart; the image in SN 36.6.

carryVoice: The line for today: only one arrow, and you don't have to fire the second. Two of nine on the mind at home.

sources.ref: Samyutta Nikaya 36.6 (Sallatha Sutta: the untaught person struck by two arrows, bodily and mental feeling; the taught disciple feels one)
Bhagavad Gita 2.14 (contacts of the senses give cold and heat, pleasure and pain; they come and go, impermanent; endure them)
Bhagavad Gita 2.20 (the self is never born and never dies)
